reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
clinicalPearls: Diagnosis now requires both an IDH1 or IDH2 mutation and whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion; without codeletion the tumour is not an oligodendroglioma regardless of morphology.
It is a tumour of adults with a predilection for the cerebral cortex and subcortical white matter, most often frontal.
Seizures are the commonest presenting feature and may precede diagnosis by years, reflecting the tumour's cortical, slow-growing nature.
Calcification is frequent and is well seen on CT, an unusual and helpful feature among diffuse gliomas.
Classic histology shows monotonous cells with perinuclear haloes, the fried-egg artefact, and a delicate chicken-wire capillary network.
The 1p/19q codeletion predicts sensitivity to alkylating chemotherapy and to combined chemoradiotherapy, underpinning a relatively favourable outcome.
Graded as CNS WHO grade 2 or grade 3, with grade 3 showing brisk mitoses, microvascular proliferation or necrosis, and CDKN2A homozygous deletion portends worse behaviour.
Even grade 3 oligodendroglioma generally outperforms IDH-mutant astrocytoma of comparable grade.
reference.pathophysiology: Oligodendroglioma is a diffusely infiltrating glioma defined molecularly by an early IDH1 or IDH2 mutation together with combined whole-arm loss of chromosomes 1p and 19q, typically arising from an unbalanced translocation. The mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase produces the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and drives a hypermethylator phenotype that reprogrammes gene expression. TERT promoter mutation and, frequently, CIC and FUBP1 mutations accompany the codeletion. The resulting neoplastic cells infiltrate cortex and white matter while retaining an indolent tempo, and higher-grade transformation is marked by increased proliferation, microvascular proliferation, necrosis and CDKN2A loss.
additionalInvestigations: contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain with perfusion and spectroscopy
1p/19q codeletion analysis to confirm the diagnosis
tissue diagnosis by resection or stereotactic biopsy
neuropsychological and seizure assessment at baseline
redFlags: clinical or radiological signs of raised intracranial pressure
new or progressive focal neurological deficit
status epilepticus or escalating seizure frequency
new nodular enhancement suggesting higher-grade transformation
reference.prognosis: Among diffuse gliomas the outlook is relatively favourable, with prolonged survival particularly in grade 2 disease, and the 1p/19q codeletion predicts chemosensitivity; nonetheless the tumour remains incurable and eventually progresses.
pitfalls: diagnosing oligodendroglioma on morphology alone without confirming 1p/19q codeletion
mistaking the fried-egg halo, a fixation artefact, for a specific diagnostic finding
overlooking calcified cortical lesions on MRI that are obvious on CT
assuming all IDH-mutant gliomas share the same prognosis and treatment
underestimating higher-grade transformation when enhancement appears

management: Confirm diagnosis molecularly with IDH1/IDH2 mutation plus whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion before planning treatment, since histology alone is unreliable; tumours are grade 2 or grade 3, there is no grade 4 oligodendroglioma

Pursue maximal safe surgical resection as the principal treatment, coordinating timing with radiotherapy and chemotherapy since upfront radiotherapy can reduce brain plasticity needed for later staged resection
Consider giving chemotherapy first in partially resectable tumours to allow response and plasticity before a later staged resection

For grade 3 (anaplastic) codeleted disease, use postoperative combined chemoradiotherapy rather than radiotherapy alone, given a durable survival benefit for combined therapy over radiotherapy alone in this molecularly defined population

Use an alkylating-agent-based chemotherapy regimen with radiotherapy for codeleted anaplastic disease, since this combination is associated with roughly double the survival of radiotherapy alone in this subgroup
Do not substitute chemotherapy alone for radiotherapy in newly diagnosed disease, as chemotherapy-only strategies are unproven and associated with more progression outside a trial setting
Weigh the long-term cognitive toxicity of radiotherapy against benefit given the long survival horizon typical of this tumour, particularly in lower grade disease

Consider watchful waiting after resection in select lower-risk patients, while recognizing that CDKN2A/B homozygous loss, incomplete resection, large tumour size, and midline crossing suggest a less favourable course

For grade 2 disease, discuss early postoperative radiotherapy versus deferring to progression, since early radiotherapy improves progression-free survival and one-year seizure control without a clear overall survival difference
At recurrence after radiotherapy, offer chemotherapy since most patients with anaplastic oligodendroglioma respond
Consider switching to temozolomide, an oral alkylating agent, at first recurrence after progression on an alkylating combination regimen, given comparable efficacy and better tolerability
Regard IDH1-targeted therapy and IDH1 vaccine approaches as investigational for this tumour rather than standard of care, since oligodendroglioma-specific outcome data were not established
Monitor with periodic contrast-enhanced brain MRI to detect progression or higher-grade transformation, and manage seizures with antiseizure medication as an ongoing need

Refer urgently to neuro-oncology or neurosurgery for new or progressive focal deficits, escalating seizures or status epilepticus, raised intracranial pressure signs, or new nodular enhancement suggesting higher-grade transformation, and manage all patients within a multidisciplinary neuro-oncology framework with supportive and palliative input introduced over time
